question: persister
prompt:
Research question: "What measurements or analyses would best reveal why a small fraction of genetically identical cancer cells survive targeted drug treatment?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

Work in two steps. First, in the candidates field, brainstorm 20 candidate ideas, one line each, covering as wide a range as you can. Then select the 5 candidates that best combine being non-obvious with being feasible and informative, and develop those as your ideas.

ideas.title: Sibling-split heritability clock
ideas.description: Separate pairs of related cells at defined numbers of generations apart (via dilution cloning or imaging-tracked micro-colonies), then treat one relative and score the other's descendants, measuring how the correlation in survival between relatives decays with generational distance. This converts the vague notion of a 'non-genetic state' into a quantitative heritability half-life, and distinguishes a state that is reset every cell cycle from one that persists for many divisions.

ideas.title: Cross-drug identity test with shared lineage barcodes
ideas.description: Barcode one population, split it into arms challenged with mechanistically distinct targeted agents, and ask whether the surviving barcode sets overlap more than chance. Strong overlap implies a general drug-tolerant state (slow cycling, apoptotic unpriming), while disjoint sets imply drug-specific priming such as pathway-specific expression, and the two imply completely different therapeutic strategies.

ideas.title: Decomposing survival into death, division, and arrest
ideas.description: Use week-long live imaging with an apoptosis/caspase reporter and automated tracking to measure, per surviving lineage, the death rate, the division rate, and the duration of arrest under drug. This distinguishes cells that never engage apoptosis from cells that die more slowly and from cells that keep proliferating outright, which are often conflated in endpoint colony counts.

ideas.title: Separating state frequency from state fitness in a modifier screen
ideas.description: Run a CRISPR or small-molecule modifier screen with two independent readouts: the fraction of cells entering the primed state (scored by a reporter or marker before treatment) and the survival probability conditional on being primed. Hits that change entry rate point to the regulators that generate the rare state, while hits that change conditional survival point to the effectors that execute it; a conventional resistance screen cannot tell these apart.

ideas.title: Per-cell drug exposure as a rule-out measurement
ideas.description: Measure actual intracellular drug levels cell by cell using a fluorescent drug analog, a target-engagement reporter, or mass-spec imaging, and correlate exposure with fate. This tests the mundane but rarely excluded possibility that survivors differ in uptake, efflux, or local drug access rather than in signaling state, and any residual fate variation after conditioning on exposure is a cleaner estimate of true state-driven survival.

candidates: Twin/sibling split assay: split clonal pairs at increasing numbers of generations apart, treat one half, and measure how fast survival correlation between relatives decays
Barcode the same population before challenge with two different targeted drugs in separate splits to ask whether identical lineages survive both or each drug has its own primed set
Long-term live imaging with an apoptosis reporter to decompose 'survival' into reduced death rate, division during treatment, and drug-tolerant arrest
Perturbation screen scored on two separate readouts: the frequency of cells entering the primed state versus the per-primed-cell probability of surviving
Per-cell drug exposure measurement using a fluorescent drug analog or mass-spec imaging to test whether survivors simply receive less drug
Retrospective isolation of pre-resistant cells by marking rare high-expressors before treatment and profiling them
Single-cell ATAC on prospectively marked primed cells to ask whether priming is chromatin-encoded or purely transcriptional noise
Live single-cell ERK/AKT biosensor traces before drug addition correlated with eventual fate
Intron/nascent RNA FISH on candidate resistance genes to test whether the rare state is a transcriptional burst versus a stable high state
Spatial analysis of where survivors sit relative to local cell density, colony edges, and dying neighbors
Conditioned-media and co-culture swaps to test paracrine rescue of neighbors by rare cells
Single-cell WGS or deep targeted sequencing of survivors to rule out pre-existing mutations and CNVs
Single-cell BH3 profiling or mitochondrial priming measurement before treatment, linked to fate
Cell-cycle phase and quiescence-depth reporters at the moment of drug addition versus outcome
Memory-decay experiment: isolate survivors, withdraw drug, re-challenge at a time series to measure how long the resistant state persists
Metabolic imaging (NAD(P)H, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial membrane potential) as a pre-drug fate predictor
Dose-response and schedule titration to separate tolerance thresholds from true resistance
Single-cell protein measurement of the drug target and pathway nodes to test whether priming is protein-level rather than mRNA-level
Photoconvertible tagging of individual cells during imaging followed by retrieval and sequencing
Image-based sorting on morphology/size features to test whether survivors are predictable from cell shape alone
